title: Survive the next ten years, lifespan could extend by 50 years
dek: His logic: within 8 to 10 years, medical progress will accelerate to a critical point where each year lived brings new therapies extending lifespan by more than a year—this is longevity escape velocity.
why: For anyone wanting to understand how far AI can push aging research and new drug development; most predictions rest on his individual case and a few studies, lacking large-scale validation.
who: Doctors, researchers, and longevity enthusiasts interested in AI drug discovery, digital twin clinical trials, or which large language models to use for diagnostic assistance.
skip: The final few minutes on how he documents research on X and podcast closing pleasantries—low information value, skippable.

points.h: Longevity escape velocity means each year returns more than a year
points.body: Unutmaz cites Aubrey de Gray's concept of ‘longevity escape velocity’: within about 8 to 10 years, medical progress will accelerate to where each year lived provides access to new therapies extending lifespan by more than a year. He gives GLP-1 drugs as an example—already adding 5 to 10 years for obese and chronically ill patients, with effects compounding. Eventually people in their 80s and 90s could return to the physiology of their 30s and 40s, potentially adding 50 to 100 years total.

points.h: Digital twins will compress clinical trials to weeks
points.body: He envisions a ‘digital twin’: integrating a person's genome, metabolome, immune system, microbiome and all other data into an AI model, simulating drug response first in the virtual body, then running verification only on the small fraction of humans where AI predicts 100% efficacy—compressing years-long clinical trials to months or even weeks. He thinks this is achievable within 5 to 10 years, with the ultimate goal of ‘treatment-on-demand’: after AI analyzes your genome, you order from a factory and receive your personalized drug the following week.

points.h: AGI's first level has already been achieved
points.body: Unutmaz breaks AGI into tiers, judging by whether knowledge learned in one domain can transfer to completely unrelated domains. He says if you gave GPT5 Pro a biology experiment and asked it to redesign it as a video game, it could do it—proof in his view that ‘first-level general artificial intelligence’ has been achieved. Further tiers require persistent memory, self-learning, and ‘physical intelligence’ emerging from the physical world before reaching true superintelligence.

points.h: The only existential threat is humanity itself
points.body: Against the pessimistic view that AI is an existential risk, he counters with a thought experiment: imagine a parallel world where anyone with IQ above 100 is dangerous and must be imprisoned or killed. That world would have no vaccines, none of what we have now. He argues that historically, human violence causes more suffering than anything else; AI is an enabling tool, not a replacement. The real threat is how humans misuse it.

points.h: GPT 5.5 Pro has crossed the intuition threshold
points.body: He tested it with 30 years of accumulated lab intuition: give the model a complex experiment already done with known results, and ask it to predict the outcome independently. Earlier models hit about 90% accuracy, but GPT 5.5 Pro, after 112 minutes of reasoning on a massive immunology dataset and writing a 40-page report, achieved 98% accuracy—precision he'd bet his own money on. For the first time, the intuition layer he once found ‘mysterious’ has been crossed by a model.

points.h: Personalized cancer treatment requires AI to design individual therapies
points.body: He cites an Australian computer scientist who sequenced her dog's melanoma tumor and submitted it to AI, which designed an mRNA molecule to train the dog's immune system to recognize tumor mutations. Synthesized and deployed within three months, the tumor began to recede and the dog survived. He expects that different personalized therapies could emerge for every cancer subtype—thousands of variants—with AI selecting which one each person needs from the mutation map.

points.h: Disease prediction now enables prevention in healthy people
points.body: He mentions a retrospective study using the UK Biobank (500,000 people's data) where an older model analyzing extensive biological data could predict roughly 1,000 diseases that would eventually occur in healthy people—and those people did develop those diseases later. He stresses current medicine is ‘sick care’—treating illness after it arrives—but predictions like these enable intervention through lifestyle or diet changes before disease forms.

points.h: Epigenetic clocks significantly overestimate aging reversal
points.body: Skeptical of the growing use of Horvath and other epigenetic aging clocks to measure ‘reversal of aging’, he notes these blood tests mainly reflect shifts in the ratio of young naive T cells to senescent ones, not whether skin, liver or brain actually rejuvenated. He warns future companies may claim aging reversal based solely on improving this one immune marker in their drug.
